newsitem.title: USA: American, pilots meet to flesh out new labor pact.
newsitem.headline: American, pilots meet to flesh out new labor pact.

text.p: American Airlines and its pilots union met Thursday to flesh out details of their tentative contract agreement aimed at ending a lengthy labour dispute and averting a strike next month.
President Clinton hailed the tentative pact, saying labour-management cooperation helped the United States compete more effectively in the global marketplace.

No details of the tentative accord reached Wednesday were announced, and there were no indications whether the deal was more or less favourable for the pilots than recommendations issued Wednesday by the Presidential Emergency Board that was created to press the two sides to come to terms.
Negotiators for American, the nation's second largest airline, and the Allied Pilots Association met to iron out details before the deal is presented to the union's board on Friday.
APA said the deal was an "agreement in principle" and that more work needed to be done before it could be presented to the union's board.

Clinton, meeting with Russian President Boris Yeltsin in Helsinki, Finland, said in a statement, "I want to commend the management of American Airlines and the leadership of the Allied Pilots Association for their commitment to each other and to the travelling public."

The president added that it spoke well of the two sides that they reached their pact more than five weeks before the end of a "cooling off" period during which the pilots could not strike and American could not lock them out.
He also praised the emergency board mediators who helped the parties reach their accord, saying "This settlement would not have been possible without their leadership and hard work."

Donald Carty, president of American, said after the deal was reached Wednesday: "We are pleased to have a deal. While it does not give us all we had hoped for, we very much wanted to resolve this matter."

The emergency board, formed by Clinton on Feb. 15, called for a 6.5 percent pay raise along with stock options and job protection for APA pilots when American buys new, small commuter jets for its regional carrier, American Eagle.

Wages and who will fly the new jets -- APA pilots or lower-paid Eagle pilots -- have been the key issues in the dispute that erupted briefly into a strike at midnight on Feb. 14, which was ended when Clinton formed the emergency board.
Who flies the new jets has remained a contentious issue.

Aside from the parties directly involved, Boeing Co. also has a vital interest in the talks. American has agreed to buy new Boeing jets worth $6.5 billion, but only if the pilots ratify a new contract.
Even if the union's board approves the contract, ratification by its 9,300 members remains far from certain.

The board approved a tentative contract last Sept. 2 by a vote of 10-8, but 61 percent of the pilots turned it down in January, which led to the negotiations and the brief strike last month before Clinton stepped in.
Clinton's action forced the pilots back to work for 60 days while the emergency board tried to forge a settlement and present it to the two sides.

The "cooling off" period was extended to April 28, when the APA will be free to strike. Then, only Congress can send the pilots back to work, with a law to require the pilots to accept the recommendations or enter binding arbitration.

The emergency board's proposed 6.5 percent pay increase matched American's last offer but also included options for pilots to buy AMR stock at a discount. The pilots had sought a pay raise of 11 percent.

The union wants its pilots, who earn $120,000 a year on averge, to fly the new smaller jets but American wanted to use $35,000-a-year American Eagle pilots. The union expressed concern that American would put the new, longer-range commuter jets on some of the longer routes flown by APA pilots.
American says it needs the lower-paid pilots to fly Eagle jets to compete with other low-cost regional carriers.
To meet some of these concerns, the emergency board recommended that American agree to restrictions on the number of regional jets flown, the routes they fly and airports served.
American is a unit of Fort Worth, Tex.-based AMR Corp.
